narrative:
The model predicted a 67% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3 placed you far below the average student who was accepted (who typically ranked around the 6th decile). These consistently low academic standings in law school were the main reasons the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your LSAT score of 36 was the second most important factor. Although this score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, it still nudged the prediction modestly toward passing. Unfortunately, this small positive effect was not enough to offset the much stronger negative impact of your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.5, which is noticeably lower than the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, added further concern, though it carried less weight than the top three factors. Your family income, gender, race, and full-time status played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class rank through targeted academic support and consider retaking the LSAT to boost your score. These steps would directly address the model’s main concerns. (248 words)
